title: Reading the Numbers
theme: Statistics and data: describing a set of numbers
objectives: I can explain what a sample is and why it should be representative.
I can describe a set of numbers using median, outlier, variation, and distribution.
I can explain why a correlation does not prove that one thing causes another.
I can write a short data report that quantifies a result and says how sure the numbers allow us to be.
rationale: Seventh-grade math and science both reason from data, so this unit combines three exact statistical terms (median, outlier, correlation) with the everyday words that graphs and reports lean on (data, sample, representative, variation, distribution, quantify, significant). The words follow the path of a small investigation: decide what to measure and collect data (quantify, data), choose a fair sample (sample, representative), describe what the numbers look like (distribution, variation, median, outlier), and decide what they mean (correlation, significant). Two words, sample and significant, carry other meanings that students use in daily life, so the unit contrasts the everyday sense with the statistical one. The unit builds on survey, inference, and derive from earlier work.

words.def: Facts, numbers, or measurements collected so that they can be studied.
words.ex: The data show that the plant grew faster in the sunny window.
words.ex2: Scientists collect data over many weeks before they draw a conclusion.
words.nonExample: A guess that nobody measured or counted is not data.

misuse.s: Data is a feeling that a scientist has before collecting any measurements.

words.def: A small part taken from a larger group or amount to show what the whole is like.

senses.def: A small amount of a product given to you to try.

words.ex: Researchers asked a sample of two hundred students about their favorite subjects.
words.ex2: The chemist tested a sample of water from the lake.

words.rel: a part that stands for the whole

apps.academic: A random sample gives every member of a group the same chance of being chosen.
apps.spoken: We only asked a small sample, so we're not sure yet.

cloze.s: To learn what the whole grade thinks, the council asked a random ___ of fifty students.

cloze2.s: The doctor took a blood ___ and sent it to the lab for testing.

misuse.s: A sample is the entire group, including every single member without exception.
misuse.why: A sample is only a small part of a larger group, not the entire group.

words.def: Typical of a larger group, so that it shows what the whole group is like.
words.ex: A representative sample of the town includes young people, older people, and every neighborhood.
words.ex2: The painting is representative of the artist's early style.
words.nonExample: A sample made up only of the tallest people in town is not representative.

apps.academic: A representative sample reflects the whole group, not just one kind of member.
apps.spoken: Is that group really representative of everyone?
apps.writing: Explain why your sample is representative, or admit where it is not.

cloze.s: Asking only the basketball team about school lunch would not give a ___ sample of the student body.

cloze2.s: One tidy, quiet classroom is not ___ of how loud the whole school can be at recess.

misuse.s: The sample was representative because it included only the tallest people in town.
misuse.why: A representative sample reflects the whole group; choosing only one kind of person is not representative.

visual.alt: A mixed group of people beside a target.

words.def: A difference or change from one case or time to another.
words.ex: The data showed little variation, because nearly every student slept between eight and nine hours.
words.ex2: There was a lot of variation in how tall the sunflowers grew, from under one meter to over two.
words.nonExample: Numbers that are exactly the same every time show no variation.

apps.academic: Variation in data tells us how spread out the values are.
apps.spoken: There's a lot of variation in how people answered.
apps.writing: Describe variation by naming the smallest and the largest values.

cloze.s: There was very little ___ in the test scores; nearly every student earned between 84 and 88 points.

cloze2.s: The ___ in the heights of the sunflowers, from one meter to nearly three, surprised the gardeners.

misuse.s: The data showed a lot of variation, because every single number was exactly the same.
misuse.why: Variation means differences among values; identical numbers show no variation.

visual.alt: A bar graph with bars of different heights beside a shuffle arrow.

words.frame: There was a lot of variation in ___ because ___.

words.def: The way values or items are spread out across a range or a group.
words.ex: The distribution of test scores looked like a hill, with most students near the middle.
words.ex2: The distribution of rainfall was uneven, with the coast getting far more water than the desert.
words.nonExample: A single number that names only the middle does not describe a distribution.

apps.academic: A graph of the distribution shows where the values bunch together and where they thin out.
apps.spoken: What does the distribution of ages look like?
apps.writing: Describe a distribution by saying where most values fall and where a few lie far away.

cloze.s: On the graph, the ___ of heights was bunched near the middle, with only a few very tall or very short students.

cloze2.s: A map of the ___ of rainfall showed that the north got far more water than the south.

misuse.s: A distribution is a single number that shows no spread at all.
misuse.why: A distribution describes how values are spread out, so it cannot be one number with no spread.

visual.alt: A bar graph shaped like a hill beside a bell.

words.def: To measure or express something as an exact number or amount.
words.ex: The scientists tried to quantify the storm damage by counting every broken tree.
words.ex2: Doctors use a scale from one to ten to quantify pain.
words.nonExample: Calling the rain nice and kind of wet does not quantify it.

apps.academic: To quantify how fast a plant grows, measure its height every day.
apps.spoken: Can you quantify how much better it is?
apps.writing: Replace a vague word such as lots with a number you can quantify.

cloze.s: To ___ how much trash the school produced, the students weighed every bag for a week.

cloze2.s: Words like many and few are vague, so scientists ___ amounts with exact numbers.

misuse.s: To quantify the rainfall, she described it as nice and sort of wet without using a single number.
misuse.why: To quantify is to give an exact number or amount; a vague description does not.

visual.alt: A ruler beside a row of numbers.

words.def: The middle number in a list of numbers arranged from smallest to largest.
words.ex: The median of the numbers 3, 5, and 9 is 5.
words.ex2: Because the list had an even count of numbers, the median was halfway between the two middle ones.
words.nonExample: The largest number in the list is not the median.
words.rel: the middle of an ordered list

apps.academic: To find the median, put the data in order and find the middle value.
apps.spoken: The median score was an eighty-five.
apps.writing: Report the median when a few extreme values might make an average misleading.

cloze.s: To find the ___ of the five quiz scores, Lila listed them in order and picked the one in the middle.

cloze2.s: The ___ of 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 is 6, the number in the middle of the ordered list.

misuse.s: The median is the biggest number in the list.
misuse.why: The median is the middle value of an ordered list, not the largest.

visual.alt: A row of numbers with a target at the middle.

words.def: A value that is far away from most of the others in a set.
words.ex: In a list of quiz scores in the eighties, a score of 12 is an outlier.
words.ex2: The outlier in the data turned out to be a typing mistake.
words.nonExample: A number in the middle of the group is not an outlier.

apps.academic: Scientists check an outlier to see whether it is a mistake or a real result.
apps.spoken: That one number is an outlier; let's double-check it.
apps.writing: Name the outlier and say whether you kept it or removed it, and why.

cloze.s: Nearly everyone finished the race in about ten minutes, but one runner who took an hour was an ___.

cloze2.s: The scientist checked the ___ twice to be sure the measurement was not a mistake.

misuse.s: An outlier is a number that is exactly the same as every other number in the set.
misuse.why: An outlier is far from the other values, so a value identical to the others is not an outlier.

visual.alt: Two white circles in a row with one red circle set apart.

words.def: A relationship in which two things change together, so a change in one goes with a change in the other.
words.ex: The graph showed a strong correlation between ice cream sales and sunny weather.
words.ex2: Teachers noticed a correlation between hours of practice and free-throw accuracy.
words.nonExample: A correlation alone does not prove that one thing causes the other.

apps.academic: A scatterplot shows whether two variables have a positive or negative correlation.
apps.spoken: There's a correlation, but that doesn't mean one causes the other.
apps.writing: Say correlation, not cause, unless an experiment shows one thing causes the other.

cloze.s: The scatterplot showed a clear ___ between hours of study and test scores, since both tended to rise together.

cloze2.s: Scientists found a ___ between warm weather and ice cream sales, though that does not mean ice cream warms the air.

misuse.s: A strong correlation proves that one event definitely causes the other.
misuse.why: Correlation shows that two things change together; it does not prove that one causes the other.

visual.alt: A rising graph beside an ice cream cone.

words.frame: There is a correlation between ___ and ___, but ___.

words.def: Large or important enough to be noticed or to matter.

senses.def: In statistics, too large to be explained by chance alone.
senses.example: The difference between the two groups was statistically significant.

words.ex: The new bridge made a significant difference to the daily commute.
words.ex2: Sleeping only three hours is a significant change from sleeping eight.
words.nonExample: A change too small for anyone to notice is not significant.

apps.academic: A result is significant in statistics when chance alone is unlikely to explain it.
apps.writing: Use significant for a difference that matters, and back it up with numbers.

cloze.s: The coach said that the team's improvement over the season was ___, since they went from last place to second.

cloze2.s: A tiny change in the number of absences was not ___ enough to worry the principal.

misuse.s: A significant difference is so small that nobody could ever notice it.
misuse.why: Significant means large or important enough to be noticed, so a difference nobody notices is not significant.

words.frame: A significant change in ___ would be ___.

passage.title: How Much Sleep Do Seventh Graders Get?
paras: For her science fair project, Amira wanted to quantify something people usually describe with vague words: how much sleep seventh graders get. “Plenty” and “not enough” mean different things to different people, so she decided to collect data in hours.

She could not ask all 400 students in her grade, so she chose a sample of forty. To make the sample representative, she used the class lists and picked every tenth name instead of asking only her friends. If she had asked only the basketball team, the results might have described athletes rather than the whole grade.

The distribution of hours, shown on a bar graph, looked like a hill. A few students slept six hours, many slept eight or nine, and a few slept ten. There was real variation, but most of the numbers clustered in the middle. Amira found the median by lining up all forty answers in order and finding the middle, and it was eight and a half hours. One answer stood out: a student who slept only three hours was an outlier, so Amira checked it twice before deciding to keep it.

Next she compared sleep with quiz scores. Students who slept longer tended to score higher, so the two sets of numbers showed a positive correlation. Amira was careful, though. “A correlation does not prove that more sleep causes higher scores,” she wrote. “Students who sleep well might also eat breakfast, finish homework early, or have quieter homes.”

A statistics teacher, Mr. Silva, told her that a small difference in averages might not be significant, because a sample of forty could differ from the whole grade by chance. Amira's difference was large enough to be worth reporting, but she added that more testing was needed. “A good scientist,” she concluded, “tells readers how sure the numbers allow her to be.”

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word “representative” most nearly means
choices: typical of the whole group
expensive to collect
chosen by a government official
made up only of friends
qs.why: Amira picks every tenth name so that the sample reflects the whole grade, not one kind of student.

qs.q: Why does Amira pick every tenth name from the class lists instead of asking her friends?
choices: Her friends would not answer honestly.
Every tenth name is the easiest to remember.
It keeps the sample from being made of people who are alike, so it reflects the whole grade.
The class lists were already in order.
qs.why: The passage says asking only the basketball team would describe athletes, and her method avoids that kind of narrow sample.

qs.q: Why did Amira check the three-hour answer twice?
choices: It was the median of the data.
It was the most common answer.
It was written in pencil.
It was an outlier, far from the other answers.
qs.why: The text calls the three-hour answer an outlier, a value far from the others, so she verified it before keeping it.

qs.q: Why does Amira warn that correlation does not prove that sleep causes higher scores?
choices: Quiz scores cannot be measured.
Other factors, such as breakfast or a quiet home, could explain both results.
Students were not asked about sleep.
The sample was larger than the whole grade.
qs.why: She lists other things that could go along with both good sleep and high scores.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Sleep is the only thing that affects quiz scores.
Outliers should always be deleted from data.
A careful investigation uses a fair sample and is honest about what the numbers can show.
A science fair project needs exactly forty students.
qs.why: Amira chooses a representative sample, checks an outlier, separates correlation from cause, and says more testing is needed.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for collecting, describing, and interpreting data, read an informational passage about a student's sleep survey, and write about choosing and reporting a sample. The emphasis is on honest language: say what the numbers show, how they were gathered, and what they do not prove.

notes.va.data.n: Data is the plural of datum, and many writers now treat data as singular too. Either is acceptable here, so be consistent. Distinguish data (what was collected) from conclusions (what you decide from it).
notes.va.sample.n: Two senses: a small part used to represent a whole, and a free taste or trial. Ask students what makes a sample useful: size and fairness. Avoid saying that a bigger sample is always better; a biased large sample can still mislead.
notes.va.representative.adj: Representative is not the same as large. Have students list ways a sample can fail to represent: only friends, only one grade, only volunteers. The noun representative (a person who speaks for others) is a different use.
notes.va.variation.n: Variation is how much values differ. Use two sets with the same middle but different spread. The family includes vary, varied, and variable, which is a good link to science variables.
notes.va.distribution.n: Distribution is the overall shape of the values. Use a dot plot on the board and ask where the values bunch, where they thin out, and whether any sit alone. The verb distribute (to hand out) is related but is used differently here.
notes.va.quantify.v: Quantify means to put a number on something. Practice replacing vague words (lots, hardly any) with numbers. The family includes quantity and quantitative; link to quantitative versus qualitative data if students are ready.
notes.va.median.n: Median is the middle value of an ordered list. For an even count, take the value halfway between the two middle ones. Students often forget to order the list first. Compare with the mean only if it is part of the current math unit.
notes.va.outlier.n: An outlier is far from the rest. Do not tell students to delete it; teach them to check whether it is an error or a real result and to say what they decided. Ask how the median reacts to an outlier compared with other measures.
notes.va.correlation.n: Correlation means two things change together; it does not prove a cause. Use the ice cream and sunny weather example and ask what a third factor might be. Practice phrases such as is linked to and goes with instead of causes.
notes.va.significant.adj: Two senses: important enough to matter (everyday) and too big to be explained by chance (statistics). The statistical sense is introduced in senses; do not teach a calculation. Ask students to say what the number is significant compared with.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “Amira wants to quantify sleep, so she collects data in hours. She cannot ask everyone, so she picks a sample, and every tenth name makes it representative. The distribution looks like a hill, the median is eight and a half hours, and one three-hour answer is an outlier that she checks. She sees a correlation with scores, but she does not say sleep causes them. That is careful language.”
discuss: Which word in the unit is most likely to be misused in a news story, and how?

misconceptions: A bigger sample is always more representative.
The median is the same as the average.
An outlier is always a mistake and should be deleted.
A correlation proves that one thing causes the other.
extend: Collect a small set of data from the class (for example, minutes spent on homework), find the median, identify any outlier, and write a three-sentence report that avoids claiming a cause.
Find a news graph or headline that reports a correlation and rewrite it to avoid implying cause.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Link back to survey, inference, and derive by asking students what a survey needs to be fair, which inferences the data supports, and what they can derive from a table. Revisit median, outlier, and correlation two days later with a new data set, again at one week in a science or math lesson, and in the final grade 7 units when students analyze evidence.

needsReview: Mathematical definitions to confirm with a math reviewer: median for odd and even counts (including halfway between the two middle values), outlier as a value far from most others, correlation as two things changing together, significant (statistics) as too large to be explained by chance alone.
Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: muestra (sample), valor atípico (outlier), mediana, cuantificar, significativo, and the cognate flags.
Passage is invented; the project, the numbers (sample of forty, median 8.5 hours, three-hour outlier), and the characters are fictional and should not be read as real findings.
Sense boundary: significant lists the statistical sense under senses; sample lists the free-taste sense.
